name: Bin codes that swap into each other
brief:
A warehouse labels its bins with codes of lowercase letters. Positions count from 0. A relabeller may swap two letters that are both at even positions, or two that are both at odd positions, as often as it likes. Two codes are in the same class when one can be turned into the other this way. Return the number of classes among `codes`.

Write `count_code_classes(codes)`.

Example. In `["mnop", "onmp", "mpon", "nmop"]` the first three hold `m` and `o` at even positions and `n` and `p` at odd ones. `nmop` holds `n` and `o` at even positions, so it is alone. The answer is 2.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 100{,}000$ codes, each of 1 to 20 lowercase letters. Codes may differ in length.
$O(n \cdot L \log L)$ time is the target, where $L$ is the longest code. Comparing every pair of codes is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Two codes are in one class exactly when their even-position letters match as a multiset and so do their odd-position letters. Build that pair as a key and count the distinct keys.

examples.note: The first three share even letters m, o and odd letters n, p. The last has n and o at even positions.
A swap never moves a letter between an even and an odd position, so these two stay apart.

tests.call: count_code_classes(["".join("abcde"[(i * (j + 3) + j * j) % 5] for j in range(8)) for i in range(60000)])
count_code_classes(["".join("abcdefgh"[(i >> j) % 8] for j in range(0, 18, 3)) for i in range(100000)])

how: Submit runs 11 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: The key is the sorted even-position letters paired with the sorted odd-position letters.
Sorting the whole code is wrong: `ab` and `ba` are anagrams but no swap joins them.
One sort per code and one set, so the work is $O(n \cdot L \log L)$.

planted.code:
def count_code_classes(codes):
    return len({"".join(sorted(c)) for c in codes})
planted.slip: It keys each code by all its letters sorted, so anagrams such as `ab` and `ba` merge though no swap joins them.
It keys on the set of letters at each parity, so it drops repeats and merges `axaxb` with `axbxb`.
